NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Kanjirappally Local Event Title of the proposal: Creating MICROSPACE: A space biology–inspired digital health platform for early detection and prevention of diabetic microvascular and tissue complications.

Mission: Discovering how the human body adapts to space to develop smarter strategies for protecting human health on Earth and beyond.

summary of the proposal :Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to a unique combination of physiological stressors, including microgravity, ionizing radiation, physical unloading, circadian disruption and environmental confinement. These stressors can adversely affect cardiovascular function, vascular regulation, skeletal muscle, bone metabolism, mitochondrial bioenergetics and tissue repair. Interestingly, several of these physiological changes have parallels in chronic diabetes mellitus, particularly in individuals who develop progressive microvascular complications, peripheral neuropathy, muscle dysfunction, impaired angiogenesis and non-healing diabetic foot ulcers. MICROSPACE proposes an innovative Space-to-Earth translational health platform that integrates publicly available NASA space biology data, physiological health indicators and clinical parameters associated with diabetic complications. The platform will use data-driven analytical approaches to identify overlapping biological pathways and develop a prototype system for monitoring tissue health, detecting early warning signals and supporting personalised preventive interventions. The project will establish two interconnected applications: (i) an astronaut health-monitoring framework for identifying physiological changes associated with prolonged space missions and (ii) a terrestrial clinical application for identifying individuals at increased risk of diabetic microvascular and tissue complications. By combining space biology, clinical research, artificial intelligence, mitochondrial pharmacology and integrative healthcare, MICROSPACE aims to transform discoveries from human space exploration into innovative approaches for preventing chronic diabetic complications on Earth.

Scientific rationale :The human body undergoes substantial physiological adaptations during prolonged spaceflight. Reduced mechanical loading, altered gravity, radiation exposure and other spaceflight-associated stressors can affect multiple organ systems. People living with long-standing diabetes also experience progressive alterations in several interconnected physiological systems. Chronic hyperglycaemia, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and impaired mitochondrial function contribute to vascular and neural injury, defective tissue repair and progressive organ dysfunction. We propose that selected biological pathways involved in spaceflight-associated physiological deterioration may provide useful insights into the mechanisms underlying diabetic complications.

The major areas of potential convergence include: a. Microvascular dysfunction and impaired tissue perfusion :Spaceflight-associated cardiovascular and vascular adaptations may provide insights into the regulation of tissue perfusion, vascular function and oxygen delivery. In diabetes, endothelial dysfunction and microvascular injury compromise tissue oxygenation and nutrient delivery, contributing to peripheral tissue damage and delayed wound healing. b. Mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular energy depletion: Mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress are important determinants of cellular adaptation to environmental stress. Mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species generation are also implicated in diabetic vascular injury, neuropathy and impaired tissue regeneration. c. Musculoskeletal deterioration: Spaceflight-associated unloading promotes muscle atrophy and alterations in bone remodelling. Chronic diabetes is associated with impaired muscle function, sarcopenia and abnormalities in bone quality and metabolism. d.
